name: harp

attributes.attribute: symbol of Ireland tied in ancient times to the god the Dagda
the Dagda's harp plays only sleep, grief, and laughter and flies to kill
earliest Irish name crott, akin to the British chrotta
later triangular frame form shown on the shrine of Saint Maedoc and the Brian Boru harp

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The harp is the stringed instrument that symbols today Ireland. In ancient times people tied it to the beneficent god the Dagda. At his call the harp flew across the land and struck down anyone in its path. The Dagda's harp had only three melodies: sleep, grief, and laughter. A like legendary harp appears in the Welsh tale of Culhwch ac Olwen. Koch's encyclopedia adds a deep history. The earliest Irish word for a harp-like instrument was crott, close to the chrotta the poet Venantius Fortunatus linked to the Britons. Early Irish verse used the words crott and cruit for the instrument. Later Ireland adopted the triangular frame harp, shown on the eleventh-century shrine of Saint Maedoc and in the famous Brian Boru harp of the fourteenth century.
objective: Document the harp as the sacred instrument of the god Dagda and of Ireland.
key_results: Record the Dag's harp with its three melodies.
Note the earliest Irish word crott and its history.
Describe the triangular frame and its famous examples.
